The Seven Layers of the Cosmos

To find closure for her mother’s disappearance, 18-year-old Luna returns to the Philippines and accidentally tears open a portal to the precolonial 15th century, where she must trust strangers, outrun cutthroat pirates, and embrace her destiny as the Keeper. It is the only way she will ever find her way home to 2025.

Kath Conti is the pen name of Filipino-Spanish author Katherine Joy Continente-Roldan. Born and raised in a small village in Cabatuan, Iloilo, she earned her MA in Applied Linguistics and TESOL from the University of Portsmouth and is now pursuing a law degree with the University of London.

Babaylan (spiritual leaders) used this clay vessel to hold sacred offerings or call on ancestral spirits. During rituals, it connected the physical world to the spirit world.

A fast, sleek warship with outriggers and raised platforms for warriors. Fleets used it to control the sea lanes, raid enemies, and show their power across the islands.

A large wooden boat built from planks pegged together at the edges. People used it to migrate, trade, and cross the ocean. It stood for clan unity and the bond that held a coastal settlement together.

A powerful single-edged longsword with a fork-shaped tip on its handle. Chieftains and elite warriors used it to deliver deadly slicing blows in battle.

A wavy, double-edged dagger or sword made for close combat. It was known for its smooth piercing strikes and was linked to the owner’s spiritual authority.

A flexible, whip-like weapon used in both fighting and spiritual cleansing. People believed it could drive away evil spirits and cause terrible wounds.

A bamboo spring-spear trap set in dense forests to hunt wild animals. It is also the name of a star constellation that ancient Filipinos used to mark the start of the planting season.

A thin sheet of gold shaped to cover the eyes and nose of the dead. It protected the soul from evil spirits and showed the noble status of the deceased on their journey to the afterlife.

A carved wooden coffin shaped like a canoe. It held the body of the dead and carried their spirit across the primordial waters to the ancestral realm.

The unseen spirit guide or animal guardian bound to a babaylan. It protected the babaylan, gave divine knowledge, and accompanied them through the spirit world.

The story of The Seven Layers of the Cosmos carries readers through worlds that could not be more different, each with its own culture, rules, and traditions. It begins with Luna’s ordinary life in Spain, moves to the vibrant Dinagyang festival in Iloilo, Philippines, then goes back more than five centuries to the coastal villages of Katagman and the prosperous sultanate of Sulu in the 15th century. The seven layers of the cosmos themselves are explored on a separate page.

Chapter 1

The Departure

Luna tumbles out of an ancient clay pot into a 15th century Visayan market just as a sea raid erupts. Her phone and research files are gone. She crawls back to the pot hoping it will take her home, and finds a message from her missing mother: “Para Luna: Find the Keeper,” dated the day Dr. Ana May vanished.

Chapter 2

Always Forward

Six months earlier in Madrid, Luna rows through her grief over her mother’s six year disappearance. In her mother’s untouched study, she finds a final notebook entry marking a clay pot and the Dinagyang Festival. It sends her straight toward the artifact that will change her life.

Chapter 3

Red Sand

In the chaos of the Katagman raid, Luna helps the injured merchant Apo Uray fight off a bloodthirsty attacker. With a cart rope and a bamboo pole, she brings the raider down. She earns a powerful ally, one who knows far more about the sacred pot than he admits.

Chapter 4

Breaking Point

On festival day in Iloilo, a scar-necked man dressed as an Ati warrior follows Luna into the museum. The display case shatters, glowing symbols burn into her wrists, and a wind vortex tears open inside the pot. As the void pulls her under, her stalker warns her: “Your mother made a terrible mistake.”

Chapter 5

The Datu’s Daughter

Dayang Bulansari mistakes Luna for a skilled healer, and Luna tries to keep up the act. A blind elder shrinks from her in terror, and the ambitious apprentice Lumbanaw circles for power. When Bulanon’s sacred pot turns up on Apo Uray’s cart at sunset, suspicion falls on Luna.

Chapter 6

Little Starlings

To prove her innocence, Luna sneaks into the dead chief babaylan’s hut. She finds muddy footprints and a clay pot full of carved wooden starlings. At the funeral, a living starling meets her eyes and speaks into her mind: “The Keeper.”

Chapter 7

Death Lingers

Luna blends into the mourners on the beach while listening for whispers of dark sorcery. Instead, the villagers whisper about her. Chief guard Owak steps into the firelight and arrests her for sorcery and treason.

Chapter 8

First Light

Locked in a neck stock, Luna is promised a fair trial by Dayang Bulansari and Kilaton. Then Owak returns and attacks her. Her body erupts with light, and nine diamond Keeper tattoos bloom across her wrists.

Chapter 9

A Sorceress Must Die

Lumbanaw demands her execution in a raging storm, and Luna fights for her life with pure deduction. She exposes the poison, points to the defensive wounds, and notes the dog’s rage at Lumbanaw. A search of his pouch reveals Bulanon’s stolen starling and proves he is the killer.

Chapter 10

Destiny

With her name cleared, Luna and Bulansari walk the beach and debate destiny against free will. Bulansari opens up about her arranged marriage, while Luna feels the weight of being the Keeper. Luna dreams of a future where women choose their own paths, but her own way home stays locked.

Chapter 11

The Journey to Upper Halawod

Apo Uray drives Luna inland in a buffalo cart to begin her babaylan training. He tells her that six years ago a prophet foresaw the Keeper and set a covenant against the Pirate King in motion. His bargain is simple: help defend Katagman, and he will reveal who the prophet was.

Chapter 12

Kabatuan

Feverish and trembling, Luna arrives in an Ati village and is pulled into a spirit trance. Then raiders strike at night. She stands in a shield wall beside Kilaton and Buhawi, drives her dagger into a raider, and earns Kilaton’s silent respect.

Chapter 13

Upper Halawod

Luna trains under Apo Siday in wind, herbs, and spirit omens, but her powers are volatile and her loner habits clash with village life. Buhawi confronts her and teaches her the idea of kapwa, shared identity. Trying to survive alone, he warns, will destroy her.

Chapter 14

The Silver Thread

Apo Siday sends Luna to mend the soul of a dying boy, but her focus slips and her spell collapses. Apo Siday steps in and saves the child. Then he reveals how dark sorcerers strip souls to build hollow, unfeeling weapons.

Chapter 15

A Song to the Motherland

At a feast, Luna bonds with the village children, then sings the Philippine national anthem as pirate raids loom. She tells how her people overcame three centuries of colonization. Buhawi and the warriors answer with a thunderous oath of resistance.

Chapter 16

The Forbidden Crossing

Desperate to find her spirit companion, Luna crosses into the spirit realm alone, ignoring Apo Siday’s warnings. On a shadowed path, an invisible sigbin ambushes her. She impales it, then wakes bleeding from three claw wounds and learns that spirit wounds are real.

Chapter 17

The Enchanted Forest

Fleeing an undead maranhig, Luna leaps off a spirit cliff into a golden enchanted forest full of mythical animals. Before any can approach her, the air turns electric. The sky goddess Alunsina appears in radiant mist, and she has noticed Luna.

Chapter 18

The Price of Power

Four dark sorcerers and fifteen cutthroats attack Upper Halawod and shatter the babaylans’ golden domes. Apo Siday slaps Luna awake, and she unleashes a storm of lightning and thunder. She wins, but a dying pirate stabs Apo Siday, and Luna loses her master.

Chapter 19

Bird’s Eye View

Luna scouts the river through an egret’s eyes and plans a mangrove ambush to retake the stolen pot from Lumbanaw. The fight turns vicious. A blow to the head leaves her captured and dragged aboard a pirate warship bound for Sulu, while her friends watch helplessly.

Chapter 20

The Seven Layers of Cosmos

While her body lies bound on a pirate ship, Alunsina guides Luna’s spirit through the seven layers of the cosmos. Luna learns that the creator Laon has vanished and that Saragnayan plots a takeover. The gods cannot wield the pot. Only a mortal “human circuit,” willing to sacrifice everything, can.

Chapter 21

The Battle of Katagman

Katagman grieves five hundred dead and the fall of Datu Bangkaw. Buhawi weeps over his father as despair spreads. News arrives that Saragnayan means to possess the Pirate King, so Apo Uray rallies Kilaton and Buhawi for a bold rescue in Sulu.

Chapter 22

Feast

Chained in a Sulu slave pen, Luna is dragged to a lavish banquet hosted by Lumbanaw. He tempts her with a dark partnership, claiming he killed Bulanon to free humanity. Luna mocks his hypocrisy and his fake power, and he promises to mount her head on a spike.

Chapter 23

Market Day

Luna sends her mind into a shorebird to map the slave compound, then breaks her chains with an incantation. She slips past the auction pens, but a barking dog raises the alarm. Running for the back wall, she slams into a thorn choked fence lined with rotting severed heads.

Chapter 24

The Sultan of Sulu

Buhawi poses as a wealthy merchant, offering Kilaton as collateral to enter Sulu. At the Sultan’s feast, he dines beside covenant leader Bai Mayana and asks to inspect the female slaves as if buying weavers. All the while, he hides his true mission and finds where Luna is held.

Chapter 25

The Escape

Kilaton and Buhawi free Luna and slip through the market in stolen guard gear until the alarm gong sounds. Kilaton makes a heroic stand alone against a squad of swordsmen. It buys Luna and Buhawi time to reach the port, and costs him his freedom.

Chapter 26

Sitti

Luna wakes in a safe house with the healer Apo Sitti and her granddaughter Fatima. Believing Kilaton died because of her, she weeps and refuses to eat. Apo Sitti comforts her with goat curry and news that Bai Mayana is gathering forces for a counterstrike.

Chapter 27

The Covenant

Sleepless, Luna walks the night beach, studying the stars. Apo Sitti finds an ash gray curse creeping up her ankle toward her liver. Then comes a shock: the Pirate King and the Sultan of Sulu are brothers.

Chapter 28

Thief

In the Sulu market, Luna sees dead fishermen floating in the harbor, torn by monster claws. She tries to buy ginger and garlic to fight her curse, and a vendor accuses her of theft. She flees along the boardwalk with the Sultan’s guards on her heels.

Chapter 29

Rough Water

Apo Sitti pulls Luna onto an outrigger and sails for Marungas Island. As Luna treats her curse with turmeric paste, a violent gale snaps their paddle and flips the boat into breaking waves, and the curse flares across her skin.

Chapter 30

Shapeshifters

On Marungas Island, aswang plagues spread terror as Luna helps prepare the defenses. A warship lands, and two men who look exactly like Kilaton and Buhawi step ashore. Fearing shapeshifters, Luna draws her twin daggers in a tense standoff.

Chapter 31

The Return

Kilaton proves who he is by offering a stingray tail, whose salt is deadly to dark spirits. After Luna dodges a spear trap, she shows the warriors her parabolic mirror torches. They can cut through supernatural sea mist and turn the flagship into a weapon against sorcery.

Chapter 32

Looming Darkness

Aboard the karakoa, Luna and Kilaton prepare to face the dark armada. The curse on her arm reaches a critical point, threatening to consume her spirit. On the storm tossed deck, Kilaton binds her wounds and kisses her before they sail into the dark god’s domain.

Chapter 33

Creatures of the Cold

Under a huge dark cloud, scale armored merfolk attack the ship with high pressure water jets. Luna directs mirror torches and stingray barbs and drives them off. In a sudden vision, she sees black smoke pour into the Pirate King’s throat as Saragnayan claims his body.

Chapter 34

The Abandoned Fishing Village

Five survivors land at a deserted village littered with skeletons. Kilaton and the Sultan set off on a fifteen day march to rally two thousand covenant warriors, leaving Luna with Bai Mayana. At dawn, Kilaton holds her hands and promises to return.

Chapter 35

I Found You Only to Lose You Again

In a trance, Luna begs the Divine Council of Gods for help, and they coldly refuse. She wakes to find Bai Mayana mortally wounded by an aswang. Luna tries the soul mending chant but watches the silver thread snap. Bai Mayana’s final secret: she was once a time traveler.

Chapter 36

Bahay Kubo

Fifteen days later, Kilaton returns with fifty karakoas and two thousand warriors to storm the Pirate King’s island. In a howling gale, the team finds a single bamboo hut. Every scout sent inside vanishes, so Luna leads her core team through the door.

Chapter 37

The Doors of Desire

Inside is a realm of thousands of bamboo doors that show each warrior their deepest desires. As many give in, Luna forces doors shut and rallies her crew with a speech about future generations resisting colonization. With her leopard cat Timaan beside her, she leads the survivors toward an acacia door.

Chapter 38

Buhawi

A white antlered deer sent by Alunsina guides Luna across a swaying bridge over an abyss. Behind her, Buhawi holds a shield wall against Saragnayan’s soulless army. When black liquid eats the bridge, he cuts the last vines to save her and slides into the dark to fight alone.

Chapter 39

The Final Battle

Luna reaches the cavern where the possessed Pirate King sits on a rock throne ringed by eight levitating sorcerers. A rift tears open, spilling a divine war into the cave as dark spirits prepare to take human bodies. Luna steps into the ritual circle and touches the sacred pot to begin the final binding.

Chapter 40

The Way of Bamboo

In the pot’s trance, Saragnayan offers Luna an easy escape home and warns that resisting will destroy her body. She refuses and offers herself as the mortal human circuit. Channeling cosmic gaba through her sun tattoo, she destroys the dark god’s host, seals the rift, and saves the middle world.

Chapter 41

Temporal Displacement Disorder

Luna snaps back to the Iloilo museum at 6:00 PM on January 15, with her phone, camera, and files restored and her Keeper markings still on her skin. She meets Agent De la Cruz and embraces both her growth and her mother’s legacy. No longer the guarded runaway she was, Luna agrees to help the government with a new cosmic portal on Thitu Island.

In the old Visayan view of the world, the universe has seven layers. They are not stacked like the floors of a building. They exist side by side in the same space, so the spirit world is all around us, even if we can’t see it. Humans, nature spirits, ancestors, and gods share the same land, sea, and sky, each in their own layer.

Layer 1

The Base Layer

The foundation of the universe. Nobody lives here. Four giant bamboo pillars rest on it and hold up the world, like the posts of a bamboo house. Old stories say a giant hog under the earth rubs against them and causes earthquakes.

Layer 2

Tubignon

the Water Realm

The world of the deep sea, the ocean floor, and the rivers. Sea spirits and merfolk (kataw) rule here and use fish as their messengers.

Layer 3

Idalmunon

the Underground Realm

The world deep inside the earth. Its spirits are easily disturbed by people digging or mining, and they may make humans sick when they are angered.

Layer 4

Lupan-on

the Middle World

The surface of the earth, shared by humans and many nature spirits. We see fields, forests, and rivers, and spirits live in the very same places. Most trouble between humans and spirits starts when people trespass without knowing it.

Layer 5

Kahanginan

the Air Realm

The sky just above the earth, home to flying spirits that stir up the wind and the storms.

Layer 6

Ibabaw-non

the Upper Realm

The home of ancestors, whose spirits stay close to their families. The babaylan, the spiritual leaders, travel here in trance to speak for the living.

Layer 7

Langit-non

the Highest Heaven

The highest layer, the home of the Supreme Creator. The Creator stays distant from everyday human affairs and works through lesser divine beings and the laws of nature.

Every chapter of The Seven Layers of the Cosmos is grounded in research. The customs, beliefs, and daily life of the story’s world come from historical records, folklore, and the work of scholars who have studied precolonial Philippine culture. These are the main sources behind the story.

The Boxer Codex is a late 16th century Spanish manuscript, illustrated by hand, that records the appearance, dress, customs, and beliefs of the peoples of the Philippines and nearby regions at the time of first contact, including the tattooed Visayans the Spanish called “Pintados.”

Read the Boxer Codex

The Hinilawod is a chanted epic of the Sulod people of Panay, about 29,000 verses long and taking two to three days to perform, that tells of the sky goddess Alunsina and her demigod sons.

Listen to the epic chantRead the article

The Maragtas is a work by Pedro Monteclaro, translated as History of Panay from the first inhabitants and the Bornean immigrants, from which they descended, to the arrival of the Spaniards. It tells how ten datus fled the tyranny of Rajah Makatunaw in Borneo and landed on Panay, where they bartered with the Ati chief Marikudo for the plains and valleys of the island, offering gold in return. The legend names Datu Puti as their leader, along with Sumakwel, Bangkaya, Paiburong, and others. The book also describes the customs, clothing, marriages, funerals, and timekeeping of the early Visayans. It describes the formation of the Confederation of Madya-as under Sumakwel. The legend also lies behind the festivals of Ati-Atihan, Dinagyang, and Binirayan.

Read the articleWatch the video

Before Spanish contact, the Visayans covered their bodies with tattoos known as batok. The Spaniards called them “Pintados,” the painted ones, and the Boxer Codex (1590) shows bold lines running up the legs and back, with matching floral designs on the chest and buttocks. These tattoos were symbols of tribal identity and kinship, as well as bravery, beauty, and social or wealth status. A tattoo was a mark of bravery not only in battle but also in enduring the pain to receive it. Each mark told a story, and the wearer carried it for life.

Read the article

Boats were the lifeblood of the precolonial Visayas. The balangay was built by joining planks edge to edge with pins, dowels, and fiber lashings, with no nails. The master shipwright was called a pandáy. Building a boat often involved religious rituals, from choosing the trees for timber to ceremonies before a voyage. The balangay carried families, trade, and warriors across the islands. The karakoa was a very large outrigger warship, about 25 meters long, with fighting platforms for warriors and platforms for the paddlers. Karakoa and balangay warships were regularly used for raiding, called mangayaw, by Visayan warriors. Boats also carried a spiritual meaning. In Visayan mythology, the deity Magyan uses a boat to ferry the souls of the dead.

Read the article

The kampilan and the kalis were the two great swords of the precolonial Visayas. The kampilan is a long, single-edged sword with a blade that widens toward the point and a forked handle. The kalis has a double-edged blade, usually straight at the tip and wavy near the handle, and unlike the Javanese keris it is a sword, not a dagger.

Philippine National Museum

While writing the aftermath of the battle, I listened to “Ili-ili Tulog Anay,” a Visayan lullaby. It is a song to soothe a child to sleep, but to me it sounds like grieving.

The Visayas had its own ancient writing system, a syllabic script related to the Baybayin.

Themes

  • Kapwa (Shared Identity)

    People are meant to live in connection with others. No one can survive, or keep their spirit whole, alone. Recognizing others as part of yourself is what makes you human.

  • Self-Reliance as Armor

    Luna protects herself by staying distant and never depending on anyone. Over the story, she learns that surviving alone is a dangerous illusion.

  • Three Values of Community

    • Pakikisama: Keeping harmony with others.
    • Pakikibagay: Bending like bamboo without breaking.
    • Pakikiisa: Standing together in true solidarity.

  • Loyalty and Self-Interest

    People ally with each other for different reasons. Some, like Apo Uray and the Sultan of Sulu, act out of practical need. Others, like Lumbanaw, betray everyone for their own gain.

  • Utang na Loob (Debt of Gratitude)

    Deep bonds and brave choices are held together by a voluntary promise to honor what others have sacrificed, and not by force or orders.
